item.title: China's top grain-producing province goes customized
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
HARBIN, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Though harvest remains more than three weeks away in the golden rice fields of Heilongjiang, China's top grain-producing province, most of this season's crop has already found a buyer. For decades, the routine was simple: consumers bought whatever was planted. Now, a growing number of enterprises are securing orders even before a single seed is sown. As China's top grain-producing province for 16 consecutive years, Heilongjiang is advancing into a new era of demand‑driven, custom‑tailored farming. CUSTOMIZED GRAINS In the fields of Qiaofu Dayuan Agricultural Co., Ltd. in Wuchang, a renowned rice-growing area in the province, each plot designated for customized orders bears a marker with the client's name. From paddy to plate, customers can follow their rice at every major stage of production through video check-ins and a traceability system. "Previously, we mainly offered customized plots measured by mu," said Qiao Wenzhi, head of Qiaofu Dayuan. One mu, roughly 667 square meters, produces about 300 kg of rice, which is far more than an ordinary family needs in a year. "Too much rice is hard for a household to consume." Last year, the company redesigned its offering around a smaller unit: one square meter produces roughly half a kilogram of rice. Consumers can choose plots that better match their needs. On the production side, the model is equally flexible, tailored to meet different consumer preferences. Wang Huixian, vice president of Qiaofu Dayuan, said consumers can choose from green, organic or ecological planting standards, and the company organizes production accordingly. The model has grown quickly: the enterprise, a flagship company in high-quality rice production, has about 180,000 mu under customized contracts, with sales exceeding 1 billion yuan (about 147.52 million U.S. dollars). The trend extends well beyond rice. Heilongjiang Heliang Agriculture Co., Ltd., a company offering diversified products, for example, has expanded customization to grains and beans. "People's health awareness is growing, and consumption patterns are changing. Many customers want personalized services," said Liu Dandan, deputy general manager of Heliang, noting that in the first half of 2026, its customized agriculture sales exceeded 70 million yuan. "Developing customized agriculture is an effective way to make use of Heilongjiang's resources and push the transformation of the province's grain and bean industry," Liu added. DIVERSIFIED CUSTOMIZED FARMING Customized farming has also expanded to vegetables and fruits. In Rendong Village of Dongfeng Township, rows of tomatoes hang heavy on the vines, and long eggplants gleam under the early-autumn sun. "The vegetables in this field are grown without chemical fertilizers or pesticides, and the entire plot was custom-ordered before spring planting," said Yang Meng, an official with the township. "The momentum for customized farming in the village is very strong." The vegetable field is divided by stone paths into neat squares, each about 50 square meters. Visitors move between the rows, picking produce for themselves. For 500 yuan, a consumer can customize an entire year's harvest from a single square. "Less than one hectare of land has generated more than 80,000 yuan in revenue this year, two to three times what corn planting would bring in," Yang said. In the village's greenhouses, the last batch of cherries was picked not long ago. Of the 1,730 cherry trees in the village, about 300 have been adopted by customers, with discounts for multi-year commitments and full harvest. MORE SCENARIOS, MORE INCOME Customized farming is also creating new consumption scenarios and new sources of income. At the Tonghe branch of Shiyue Daotian Group Co., Ltd., Zhang Shuang, a worker at the rice-polishing workshop, farms during the busy season and works at the company during the off-season, earning an extra 100,000 yuan a year. "The group regularly shares knowledge about food security and scientific farming methods, which I can apply to my own fields," Zhang said. He and most of the villagers sell their grain to the company. "We don't have to worry about sales." Zhao Shulan, general manager of the group's Wuchang branch, told Xinhua that customized farming is reshaping how food is sold and how enterprises operate. "From spring seed selection and fertilization to field cultivation and management, farmers under contract receive expert guidance to ensure unified standards and quality," Zhao said. The model also mixes agriculture with tourism. Consumers who adopt a plot are invited to visit during key moments, such as rice-flower blooming or harvest, to experience farming firsthand or participate in study tours. The harvested rice is then delivered in batches according to each family's needs. "Premium rice isn't just about taste. It is about the experience," said Qiao, adding that by combining product customization with experiential value, the premium for their rice has risen by up to 40 percent. Liu said Heliang has designed spring-plowing and harvest festivals, large-scale rice paddy art, as well as study tours and family activities, allowing consumers to experience farming culture and rural life firsthand and adding emotional and cultural value to agricultural products. As one of the key endeavors to ensure consecutive high yields and enhance agricultural returns, Heilongjiang's customized farming is scaling rapidly. In the first half of 2026, the province had 445 customized agriculture operators, with 1.799 million mu of customized planting bases, and contracted sales reached 5.55 billion yuan, up 85 percent year on year. To boost high‑quality growth in this sector, Heilongjiang released a three‑year action plan (2025‑2027) to support the industry through improved standards, regulation and services. ■

item.title: China revamps commercial spaces with immersive experiences to spur consumption
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
CHONGQING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Sipping tea in repurposed old movie theaters, wandering indoor rainforests while dining at modern malls, young consumers are reshaping China's retail landscape where creative, immersive enjoyment takes center stage. At the Sino-Swiss Technological Innovation Park in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, a rooftop commercial cluster "aa market" hosts dozens of independent brands, specialty restaurants, and indoor healing gardens. "I feel relaxed as soon as I come. I want to stay longer, unlike in a traditional shopping mall where everything feels fast-paced," said Sui Yu, a visitor to the site that draws on brutalist-infused industrial aesthetics. Jiang Hao, manager of the project, said stores focusing on a single product category have become magnets for niche buyers, and specialized retail is set to become a major consumer trend in the years ahead. The rise of these one-of-a-kind venues mirrors shifting consumer priorities. Across the country, various new models are emerging, weaving shopping together with culture, entertainment and leisure activities. In Gaomi City, east China's Shandong Province, famous as the backdrop for Zhang Yimou's breakout film "Red Sorghum," a themed night event offers immersive performances, interactive activities and local cultural experiences at the Red Sorghum Town. Roughly 100 km from Gaomi, visitors to the Qingdao International Beer Festival can map out their own itineraries and join a wide range of nighttime events, moving from passive onlookers to active participants. Historic buildings are also receiving new life through careful renovation and adaptive reuse. In Chongqing, Jiangling Teahouse occupies a former cinema built in the 1950s that was formerly affiliated with a state-owned factory. It keeps the original architectural structure intact while weaving in elements of traditional tea culture. "We hope to create a space that combines everyday life with memories of the past," said Long Yanji, marketing director of Chongqing Feibiao Cultural Creativity Co., Ltd. About 70 percent of the teahouse's visitors are middle-aged or elderly residents, many former workers at nearby factories or their relatives, Long said. Their patronage has breathed new life into the aging venue, which also draws young visitors and tourists. Beyond heritage-themed teahouses, established shopping complexes are reinventing themselves to match evolving consumer expectations. At The Ring shopping mall in Chongqing, visitors can stroll through an indoor tropical rainforest dotted with plants, waterfalls and streams while shopping and dining. "It is a fresh experience to enjoy the scenery and go shopping in the same place," said Liu Yaoze, a tourist from central China's Henan Province, who was visiting with his girlfriend. From repurposed historic buildings and cultural venues to immersive commercial complexes, innovative consumption scenarios are expanding the boundaries of shopping and leisure in China, which is also boosted by optimized policies. In July, China released a special plan under the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) framework to expand consumption, calling for developing novel consumption scenarios and encouraging commercial areas to adopt more immersive, interactive designs in a bid to generate lasting economic growth. China's total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, rose 2.6 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, official data showed. Services retail sales increased by 5 percent in the January-July period, while goods retail sales climbed by 1.1 percent. With further measures to expand and upgrade consumer goods consumption, the country expects to better tap the potential of its vast market, bringing total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.85 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030, according to officials with the Ministry of Commerce and the National Development and Reform Commission. ■

item.title: Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing. Chinese rescuers immediately launched all-out search and rescue operations. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest progress in China: -- Twenty-one people have been confirmed dead and 541 others remain missing after the mudslide struck the border port, according to the regional government's latest news briefing. An ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal has been identified as the cause of the mudslide. -- Power supply has been restored to the core area of the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port, the State Grid said. -- After the land route along to Gyirong Port was basically restored on Wednesday morning, large machinery is being used to clear obstacles and create working areas, followed closely by specialized firefighters conducting targeted searches and life-detection equipment verifying suspicious locations. -- More than 2,300 rescuers had been deployed. Multiple rounds of grid and blanket searches have been completed, covering a total area of about 1.59 million square meters. -- In the core affected area, a cumulative total of 336 rescuers have conducted multiple rounds of exhaustive searches, ensuring thorough coverage of every section. -- Rescuers are also collecting and registering all suspected personal belongings of the deceased and the missing to facilitate identification and handover. As of Wednesday noon, 847 items had been recovered. -- The Ministry of Emergency Management, in coordination with the Ministry of Transport, has dispatched road-reinforcement and heavy-lift equipment to the site. -- Central state-owned enterprises have mobilized personnel and machinery to the core area, working to secure power supply and support relief operations, according to the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission. -- Another batch of Chinese relief supplies and DNA experts arrived in Kathmandu, Nepal, by air on Thursday, as part of Chinese aid efforts following the deadly mudslide. ■

item.description:

Chinese President Xi Jinping paid a state visit to Egypt from Tuesday to Wednesday after attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 in Bishkek, and concluding his state visit to Kyrgyzstan. During the visit, Xi held talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi. The two heads of state jointly witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents. The two countries also issued a joint statement on further deepening their comprehensive strategic partnership. Accompanied by Sisi and his wife Entissar El-Sisi, Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan toured the Grand Egyptian Museum before departure. Produced by Xinhua Global Service■

(Xinhua/Wang Dongzhen) BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China announced on Friday its 1,274-member delegation for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, with 815 athletes set to compete across 38 sports and 369 events. Led by 36 Olympic champions, the squad has an average age of 24. Over a quarter of the athletes are 20 or under and most will be making their Asian Games debuts. Among the team staff, there are 69 overseas specialists from 24 countries and regions including Australia, Spain, France, the Netherlands and Britain. "The Asian Games represents the highest-level comprehensive sporting event in Asia and serves as a genuine test of our preparation," diver Wang Zongyuan said on behalf of the athletes. "We will showcase China's standard and strength on the regional and global stage." "Since 1982, China has topped both the gold medal and overall medal tables at 11 consecutive Asian Games editions," said Gao Zhidan, director of the China's General Administration of Sport and chef de mission of China's delegation, adding that China will strive to maintain its leading position at the Games. item.title: China to expand health insurance coverage for innovative drugs
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- China will expand national health insurance coverage for innovative drugs used to treat cancer, chronic and rare diseases, and childhood illnesses, with the goal of easing the financial burden on patients and their families. Since 2018, China has added 949 medicines to its national health insurance drug list, including 199 innovative drugs, Li Tao, deputy head of the National Healthcare Security Administration, said at a news conference on Friday. The administration plans to expand the range of innovative drugs covered by commercial health insurance. It will encourage commercial insurers to step in first to cover drugs that are not included in the basic health insurance program but offer significant clinical benefits and address important medical needs. It will also shorten approval timelines and help bring pharmaceutical innovations into clinical use more quickly, Li said. China's innovative pharmaceutical sector has grown rapidly in recent years. By 2025, China accounted for about 30 percent of the global biopharma pipeline, up from just 2 percent a decade earlier, and about one-fifth of global licensing deals, according to McKinsey research. In the first half of 2026, the total value of China's innovative drug out-licensing deals reached a record high of more than 100 billion U.S. dollars, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. ■

item.title: Letter from Gyirong: Mud, loss, scouring, a night in the heart of disaster
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
by Xinhua writer Jigme Dorje GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- As dusk settled on Aug. 31, our helicopter arrived at the destination. I jumped from the hovering aircraft a few meters above the ground, clutching my camera bag tightly against my chest, into a vast stretch of mud. Here I was, right in the heart of the disaster-hit zone, five days after a fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, claiming 21 lives and leaving 541 others missing as of midday Sept. 2. I came with a colleague. As a photojournalist, reporting from the scene is my professional calling. The moment my feet touched the ground, they sank deep into the mud. My legs were locked in place, while my upper body swayed for a moment before I regained my balance. A moment before, as the helicopter was descending, I looked through the window and saw what appeared to be a stretch of flat ground completely covered in mud. Only after landing did I realize just how deep it was. I tried to pull my legs free. The mud seemed to pull back. I struggled for a while, but could barely move. We were among the few reporters flown by helicopter directly into the disaster zone. At that time, the overland route into the core affected area remained inaccessible due to serious damages caused by the mudslide. Excavators were working around the clock to clear and reopen the lifeline. The first team of 141 rescuers, as well as a high-altitude helicopter, arrived at the port on the morning of Aug. 27. The next day, two teams, comprising 21 people and a search dog, became the first professional rescue teams to reach the core rescue zone at the border gate. "You're reporters, right?" a firefighter asked. "This is the last helicopter today. You're not going back tonight?" "Yes," I told him. "We're reporters." When I looked around, it struck me that I had lost count of how many times I had been to Gyirong Port. One visit remains particularly vivid in my memory. On that trip, I stayed at a small guesthouse run by villagers in Jifu Village, halfway up a mountain in Gyirong Town. I woke up the next morning to the chirping of birds. Still half asleep, I looked out the window to see a sea of clouds stretching across the valley below. I could hear people chatting and laughing nearby, including a Nepali staff member speaking Mandarin in a slightly halting voice. That was Gyirong Port as I remembered it. Now, in the middle of the devastated landscape, a square concrete platform appeared to be the only remaining structure left visible. It was the reservoir that had supplied drinking water to port staff members and residents. On the lid of the former reservoir, covering several dozen square meters, firefighters who had been among the first to reach the disaster zone had pitched a small red tent. It was barely large enough for the temporary camp of more than a dozen firefighters. With a shovel in hand, my colleague and I dug out a patch of relatively level ground beside the firefighters' tent, just large enough for a single-person tent. That was where we spent the night. Then we picked up our cameras and got back to work. Rescuers were spread across the disaster zone, searching through the mud. We interviewed and photographed several of them as they worked. As darkness fell, rescuers gradually returned to the tents, exhausted. I looked toward the foot of the mountain. One rescuer was still there, head bowed, moving slowly through the darkness, searching. By 9 p.m., it was completely dark. More and more rescuers returned to the camp to rest. Some sat down and began scraping mud from their boots. When an ethnic Tibetan firefighter sat down and pulled off his socks, we saw that his feet had been soaked in muddy water for so long that the skin had turned pale and wrinkled. Heavy machinery rumbled through the night, clearing and repairing the road, while the headlamps of crews working to restore power and communications flickered continuously in the distance. The rescuers were getting ready to eat and invited us to join them. They had pan-fried buns with braised meat. Drones had been employed to air-drop supplies to these rescuers. "This is our first meal today," an immigration police officer said. As we talked, they recalled what had happened the night before. A huge boulder had fallen from the mountain across the Gyirong Zangbo River. They had heard a deep, muffled cracking sound. Then came a loud crash as the rock plunged into the river. "The noise was enormous," one of the rescuers said. "And the splash from the rock hitting the water scared us so much that none of us dared to sleep that night." Before we went to bed, another immigration police officer pointed toward a place not far from our tent. "If anything happens, climb up this way immediately," he told us. "Grab that metal railing over there." It was the escape route. Our little patch of level ground had been carved out of the mud by hand. However, a downpour that night turned our tent into a small pond. I woke suddenly in the middle of the night, and found there was water everywhere. I shifted my body, pulled the opening of my sleeping bag tightly around me and forced myself to go back to sleep. The next morning, when we got up, the rescuers were already preparing to head out. We emptied the water from our tent and began clearing our things. The clothes we had used as pillows the night before were completely soaked. Seeing this, a firefighter brought us a set of rescue clothes and urged us to put them on. I stepped outside and looked back toward Gyirong Town. Six or seven hundred meters away, excavators were already at work. Another day had begun. In the heart of the disaster zone, rescuers once again scoured areas they had already searched several times for the missing. They were firefighters in orange, immigration police in dark blue uniforms, disinfection workers in disease-control gear, and police officers carrying cameras and notebooks. At first, everyone was searching for survivors. They called out again and again. They turned over debris and dug through the mud, searching every possible place. Then, slowly, painfully, everyone began to confront a reality that no one wanted to accept. At around 10 a.m., rescuers paused their work and stood in silence in a brief memorial service to mourn the victims. Then, they put on their safety helmets and marched again into the mud. ■

item.title: China commemorates 81st anniversary of victory against Japanese aggression
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- People across China held commemorative activities on Thursday to mark the 81st anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-1945) was the first to break out and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War. Over 14 years, some 35 million Chinese were killed or wounded. Japan officially surrendered on Sept. 2, 1945, by signing the Instrument of Surrender. The war marked China's first complete victory against foreign aggression in modern times. Through immense sacrifice, the Chinese people made a major contribution to the salvation of human civilization and the defense of world peace. In 2014, China's national legislature designated Sept. 3 as Victory Day of its War of Resistance. Last year, China held grand commemorative events in Beijing on Sept. 3 to mark the 80th anniversary of the victory, including a military parade in Tian'anmen Square. On Thursday, a symposium was held in Beijing to commemorate the 81st anniversary. Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event. About 200 people took part in the symposium, including veterans of the war, relatives of wartime commanders and fallen soldiers, and international friends who contributed to China's victory, as well as representatives of their families. Officials, young military personnel, and student representatives spoke at the event, vowing to remember history, honor fallen heroes, cherish peace, and build a better future. In Harbin, capital of northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, a series of activities commemorating the hard-won victory 81 years ago was held at the Northeast China Revolutionary Martyrs' Memorial Hall. Representatives from government agencies, businesses, military units, schools and social organizations attended a memorial event and paid silent tribute to those who fell in the War of Resistance. They also visited an exhibition featuring wartime relics to learn more about the historical significance and contemporary relevance of the spirit of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army (NAJUA). For 14 years, the soldiers of NAJUA fought in extreme conditions, suffering severe food and clothing shortages while facing overwhelming enemy superiority. Yet they still inflicted heavy losses on Japanese forces, making an indelible contribution to the World Anti-Fascist War. "We commemorate the victory so that we do not forget history," said Tong Guobo, head of the memorial hall. "The NAJUA spirit -- of unwavering faith, deep patriotism, and dauntless courage -- has taken deep root in northeast China, inspiring generations to forge ahead." At the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders in east China's Jiangsu Province, people took part in poetry readings and historical reenactments, bringing to life the harrowing stories of that dark chapter for the audience. "Both my parents were survivors of the Nanjing Massacre, and we lost six family members to the Japanese forces in 1937," said Cao Yuli, who was participating in the event. "We should always remember the past and value the peace we enjoy today," said Zhang Xinjue, a student choir member during the commemorations. In east China's Shandong Province, more than 3,000 artifacts that bear witness to the Japanese atrocities are exhibited at a private museum in Pingyin County. Among them are military postcards and letters and soldiers' diaries, as well as photographs, combat maps, and other items such as swords, helmets, and gas masks. Han Guangyou, the 65-year-old curator of the museum, has spent more than four decades amassing these artifacts from across China. "These exhibits stand as undeniable proof of the war crimes committed by imperial Japan," he said. The museum now receives more than 20,000 visitors annually. Han is currently collaborating with several universities to catalog, digitize and research the collection. "These stark exhibits serve as a sobering reminder for young people to remember the lessons of history and strive to build a stronger China," Han said. "Today's world is far from peaceful," said Zhang Shaoduo, an associate researcher at Shanghai International Studies University. "These commemorative events remind people across the globe that a stronger China remains a pillar of world peace." Also on Thursday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urged Japanese right-wing forces to adhere to the path of peaceful development, in response to Japan's record-high defense budget request for the 2027 fiscal year. "Our solemn message to Japanese right-wing forces: the right way forward for Japan is to fulfill its international obligations, fully remove the pernicious influence of militarism, and keep to peaceful development," Guo told a regular press briefing in Beijing. ■

item.title: Across rivers and ridges -- China ensures school access for children
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
* In 2022, a 268-meter-high elevator and an aerial cable car system came into service, giving children from the deep mountains a "sky shuttle" to the clifftop school. A second elevator, rising 288 meters, opened at the end of July this year as visitor numbers grew. * Across China, governments are tailoring school transport to local needs, finding different ways to close the distance between home and school. * The efforts, backed by national policy, reflect a broader commitment -- ensuring that geography does not determine a child's access to education. KUNMING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- At age 12, Lei Xin had already mastered a skill most adults would never attempt: navigating a treacherous cliffside trail in the dark -- not for adventure, but to go to school. For years, reaching school meant a three-hour trek for Lei and his peers from Nizhuhe Village in Xuanwei City, southwest China's Yunnan Province. The village sits at the bottom of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon near the border with Guizhou Province, while their school is perched more than 500 meters above them on the cliffs. Children used to leave home well before sunrise, often returning exhausted. For parents, the daily trek was a source of constant worry. Now, the most daunting stretch of the route Lei once took to school can be covered in just 57 seconds, with a new 288-meter-high cliffside elevator whisking students up the canyon wall at five meters per second. Lei's story is not unique. Across China's vast, often rugged frontier regions, millions of children face long, perilous journeys to school. From sheer cliffs to winding rivers, the obstacles vary, but so do the solutions. The efforts, backed by national policy, reflect a broader commitment -- ensuring that geography does not determine a child's access to education. CROSSING EVERY DIVIDE Guanzhai Primary School, perched on the cliffs above, serves children from surrounding mountain communities, including four in Nizhuhe Village. Cut off from the school above by sheer cliffs, the children had to follow a rudimentary trail carved into a rock face hundreds of meters high. Narrow and steep, strewn with loose gravel, the trail had sections barely half a meter wide. The steepest stretches required them to climb by hand. "Back then, I wasn't afraid my child would be tired. I was afraid something might happen to him on the way," said Zhao Suzhen, the mother of Lei, who had accompanied him along the treacherous trail countless times over the years. The change came with the development of the Nizhu River Grand Canyon scenic area. In 2022, a 268-meter-high elevator and an aerial cable car system came into service, giving children from the deep mountains a "sky shuttle" to the clifftop school. A second elevator, rising 288 meters, opened at the end of July this year as visitor numbers grew. Together, the two elevators can carry up to 1,200 passengers per hour, significantly boosting the scenic area's capacity while eliminating the congestion that once forced students to compete with tourists for rides during peak seasons. Now, the entire journey from the village to school takes about 30 minutes. Students take a shuttle bus to the foot of the cliff, ride an elevator, then continue by cable car to reach the school. On Aug. 30, as many primary and secondary schools across Yunnan welcomed students back for the new semester, Lei once again boarded his unusual ride. Stepping into the new elevator, he watched the numbers on the display tick upward. "The first elevator takes 90 seconds. This one, 33 seconds faster," he said, sharing his calculation. "I feel like an immortal carrying me through the sky." Free for local students and villagers, the "sky shuttle" also features dedicated student passages, with police officers and staff on hand during peak hours to keep the children safe. By the end of August, the service had safely carried nearly 1,000 student trips between the village and school. More than 500 km away from Puli Township, which administers Nizhuhe Village, another group of children in Yunnan began the school day on the water. At a ferry crossing in Banda Village of Bo'ai Town, located in a reservoir area, village official Liang Guoyou arrived early in the morning to help students board. One by one, the children stepped onto a ferry that carried them across the water. It's their version of a "school bus." The journey was not always this secure. "Years ago, privately operated ferries lacked unified standards, and safety was a constant concern," Liang said. Since 2021, local authorities have worked with schools, parents and transport officials to build a coordinated school transport system. Seven dedicated ferries now serve 12 crossings across the township for 329 primary and secondary school students and preschoolers. For 55-year-old ferryman Wei Jinlin, the difference could not be starker. "When I was young, getting to school meant walking nearly 20 kilometers to town," he said. "Now the children can take the ferry. It's much safer and far more convenient." According to local authorities, the ferry routes have safely carried students more than 147,000 times over the years, covering over 70,000 kilometers in total. Across China, governments are tailoring school transport to local needs, finding different ways to close the distance between home and school. In March, mountainous Chengkou County of southwest China's Chongqing Municipality launched a "Hope Line" school bus service, with 33 dedicated routes now in operation. The service uses fixed routes combined with flexible pickup points to tackle the "last mile" challenge for students living in scattered rural communities. In Panxi Town, Guizhou, authorities faced similar challenges reaching students scattered across remote areas and recently surveyed the travel needs of 121 students before launching three customized school bus routes. Four vehicles now connect eight villages, providing point-to-point service during school hours. BEYOND SCHOOL RIDES The impact, it turns out, goes far beyond the ride to school. Li Zhiguang, principal of Guanzhai Primary School, said that as the "sky shuttle" has made the journey less daunting and physically demanding, students become more cheerful, confident and engaged in school life. "They are more willing to speak up in class and eager to explore the wider world," Li added. They also have more time for the things they enjoy. "Now I can use those hours saved on the journey to read and exercise," said Wang Sichun, a third-grade student at the school, her voice bright. The benefits ripple outward. The "sky shuttle" has also enabled local co-development of education and rural revitalization. As the canyon's scenery and cliff elevators attracted more visitors, Zhao turned part of her home into a three-story guesthouse with 12 rooms. During peak season, bookings can be made weeks in advance. "Now I can look after my children while earning a living without leaving my hometown," she said. More villagers are following suit, opening guesthouses, selling local specialties or working as guides. Official data show that Puli Township now boasts 46 guesthouses and 159 specialty restaurants, with tourism supporting nearly 3,500 jobs. Cai Xiong, chairman of the company behind the elevator project, grew up in the mountains himself and watched generations of children make the arduous climb to school. "I know how difficult the journey can be," he said. "I hope the 'sky shuttle' can give them a safer way to school, so they can focus on their studies, pursue their dreams and one day give back to their hometown." Yang Bin, a professor at Yunnan Normal University who has long studied education development in western China, praised the local approach of repurposing cultural tourism infrastructure for public educational services. "This is not merely an improvement in transportation infrastructure. It is a safeguard of rural children's right to education, ensuring that frontier children truly have access to equitable and quality schooling," Yang said. He added that better educational conditions also support rural revitalization by helping to retain population and stabilize communities, providing a lasting social foundation for tourism and other industries. The efforts are now finding institutional backing. A national plan to build a strong country through education by 2035 calls for advancing high-quality, balanced compulsory education and greater integration of urban and rural education, while narrowing gaps among regions, schools and student groups. Earlier this year, China issued a plan to accelerate agricultural and rural modernization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), calling for stronger basic public services in rural areas. It specifically requires more balanced compulsory education and better conditions for rural schools, including necessary small-scale village schools and kindergartens. Yang noted that these efforts can help address the longstanding challenges in rural education and narrow the urban-rural development gap. "The road to school is, in many ways, the first step toward educational equity," he said. ■ (Video reporters: Xiong Xuanang and Wang Anhaowei; Video editors: Yang Zeyi, Roger Lott, Zhao Xiaoqing and Wang Han)
